newsitem.title: PERU: Peru to restart face-to-face dialogue with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru to restart face-to-face dialogue with rebels.

text.p: A long-awaited meeting on Sunday between Peru's chief negotiator and Marxist rebels still holding 74 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence has fuelled optimism "a tangible resolution" may be at hand.

Education Minister Domingo Palermo was expected to enter the besieged house on Sunday afternoon to talk to Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa. It was to be their second face-to-face meeting since the rebels stormed a diplomatic reception on Dec. 17 taking more than 500 hostages.

"I expect direct negotiations this time to be held smoothly and vigorously and bring about a tangible resolution," Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told NHK television network in Tokyo before the talks were to resume in Lima later on Sunday.

While seeking an early resolution to the standoff, Ikeda reiterated Tokyo's concern that the lives of the remaining hostages was paramount. "The most important thing is the safe release of all the hostages. This should take priority over the time element," he said.

Palermo arranged the meeting with Cerpa in a brief radio conversation witnessed by foreign reporters on Friday. The two men have not met since they held talks inside the residence on Dec. 28. They have since exchanged several written messages.
Of the hundreds of hostages it took, the MRTA has released the majority in what it has called "goodwill gestures."
The last major release of 20 hostages coincided with Palermo's first visit to the compound.

The rebels are holding on to the most valuable hostages, including dozens of Peruvian officials and the younger brother of President Alberto Fujimori, as bargaining chips to obtain their main demand, the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
Fujimori has insisted he will not give in to "terrorist blackmail" and has urged the rebels to lay down their arms and release all the captives under the supervision of a "guarantor committee."
The government has, however, floated the possibility of granting the rebels political exile abroad if they surrender.

Boosting signs of optimism Roman Catholic bishop Juan Carlos Cipriani returned to the residence for the second time in two days on Sunday and was expected to hold a mass for the captives. The visits of the bishop, a close friend of Fujimori, inside the compound have often been associated with hostage releases.
After the bishop's arrival, Red Cross official Michel Minnig, the chief mediator in the crisis, also entered the compound.
Although negotiations to end the conflict were apparently back on track, Peruvian authorities kept to their tough line against the MRTA.
"We consider it as a terrorist organisation because it causes fear, panic, chaos and destruction," Col. Alberto Sarmiento of Peru's National Police, told a news conference on Saturday.

On the outskirts of Lima Peruvians marched on Sunday in protest at the hostage-taking. Thousands of people from the capital's dusty shantytowns packed into a sports park before starting the two mile (3 km) walk towards the ambassador's residence in the leafy suburb of San Isidro.
The rebels are armed with automatic rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the diplomatic compound against a surprise attack.
